PHASE 4 · ADVANCED PRIMARY CARE CLINICAL MANAGEMENT

Week 83 — Lesson 107: Inflammatory Arthritis & Rheumatoid Arthritis Management

FNP-level goal: Recognize inflammatory arthritis and rheumatoid arthritis (RA) patterns, identify a possible septic joint or other urgent alternative, arrange timely rheumatology collaboration, and support safe disease-modifying treatment, infection prevention, function, and patient goals.

Learning Objectives

  • Distinguish inflammatory from mechanical joint symptoms while maintaining a differential that includes infection, crystal disease, trauma, osteoarthritis, and systemic autoimmune disease.
  • Recognize the red-hot swollen joint, fever/systemic illness, immunosuppression, and acute inability to bear weight as potential septic arthritis requiring urgent evaluation.
  • Describe common RA patterns, extra-articular risk, and reasons that early disease-modifying treatment and rheumatology referral matter.
  • Support safe DMARD/biologic treatment through medication reconciliation, infection screening, laboratory/organ monitoring, vaccine planning, and reproductive counseling when applicable.
  • Assess pain, fatigue, mobility, work, mood, cardiovascular risk, and patient access as part of longitudinal RA care.

Part 1 — Recognize Inflammation Without Anchoring Too Early

Inflammatory arthritis may present with swollen, warm, tender joints; prolonged morning stiffness; pain at rest; symptoms improving somewhat with movement; fatigue; and multi-joint or symmetric small-joint involvement. RA commonly affects hands, wrists, and feet but can involve larger joints and systemic tissues. These clues are not diagnostic alone. Crystal arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, reactive arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, viral arthritis, infection, osteoarthritis, trauma, and other conditions can look similar.

Ask about onset, number/distribution of joints, symmetry, stiffness duration, rash/psoriasis/nail changes, eye or bowel symptoms, preceding infection, fever, weight loss, travel/exposure, sexual history when relevant, family history, trauma, medications, pregnancy possibility, and immunosuppression. Examine for synovitis, effusion, warmth, range of motion, deformity, tendons, skin/nails, gait, lymph nodes, fever, and cardiopulmonary/ocular findings when indicated.

Part 2 — A Hot Swollen Joint Is an Infection Problem Until Proven Otherwise

Septic arthritis can rapidly damage a joint and may cause systemic illness. Acute severe monoarthritis with marked pain on active and passive range of motion, warmth, swelling, fever, bacteremia risk, immunosuppression, injection/drug use, prosthetic joint, recent procedure, or inability to bear weight requires urgent assessment. Absence of fever does not safely exclude infection, especially in older or immunosuppressed patients. Do not begin or increase immunosuppression through a routine message when septic arthritis is possible; urgent in-person evaluation, aspiration/culture pathway, and specialty/emergency involvement are needed.

Part 3 — RA Is Systemic, Not Just “Hand Pain”

RA is an autoimmune inflammatory disease that can cause progressive synovitis, erosions, deformity, pain, fatigue, disability, and extra-articular disease affecting the lungs, heart, eyes, skin, and other organs. It also increases cardiovascular risk. Early diagnosis and disease-modifying treatment can reduce inflammation and help prevent joint damage. Suspected persistent inflammatory polyarthritis, especially with objective synovitis or functional decline, warrants prompt rheumatology referral rather than months of repeated symptomatic-only treatment.

Laboratory tests such as inflammatory markers, rheumatoid factor, and anti-CCP can contribute to evaluation but are not single definitive yes/no tests. A negative serology does not erase an inflammatory clinical pattern; a positive test without compatible symptoms does not establish RA. Interpret labs with examination, timeline, imaging when appropriate, and specialist assessment.

Part 4 — Disease-Modifying Therapy: FNP Safety Responsibilities

DMARDs and biologic/targeted therapies can control inflammation and preserve function, but they have important infection, organ, hematologic, reproductive, interaction, and monitoring considerations. The rheumatology plan should specify the agent, dose, laboratory schedule, vaccination strategy, pregnancy/contraception guidance when applicable, infection precautions, and who to contact for a flare or adverse effect. The FNP reinforces that plan, checks adherence and access, reconciles every prescription/OTC/supplement, and closes laboratory and referral loops.

Before starting or changing immunomodulating therapy, required infection screening and baseline assessment depend on the medication and current guidance. During treatment, new fever, persistent cough, dyspnea, painful rash, urinary symptoms, unexplained cytopenia symptoms, severe oral ulcers, or other possible infection/toxicity should prompt timely evaluation. Do not tell a patient to simply “take the next dose as usual” when significant infection is suspected; coordinate with the prescribing rheumatology team and the patient’s acute-care needs.

Part 5 — Glucocorticoids and Pain Medicines Are Not the Long-Term Disease Plan

Glucocorticoids can sometimes be used as limited bridge therapy under an individualized plan, but prolonged exposure can contribute to infection, hyperglycemia, hypertension, osteoporosis, mood changes, cataracts, and adrenal suppression. Repeated steroid bursts for unrecognized uncontrolled inflammatory arthritis can delay definitive care. NSAIDs and analgesics may help symptoms but do not prevent RA erosions; consider renal, GI, cardiovascular, anticoagulant, pregnancy, and interaction risks.

Part 6 — Whole-Person Longitudinal Care

At follow-up, assess disease activity and function alongside fatigue, pain, hand use, gait, falls, sleep, mood, work/financial impact, caregiver responsibilities, oral health, tobacco exposure, weight, blood pressure, lipids, diabetes, cardiovascular symptoms, vaccine status, cancer screening, and reproductive goals. Occupational/physical therapy, adaptive devices, exercise within tolerance, smoking cessation, vaccination, and behavioral-health support are treatments—not optional extras.

Clinical Case

A 45-year-old has three months of symmetric swelling and prolonged morning stiffness in the MCP and wrist joints, fatigue, and difficulty opening jars. Today, one knee suddenly becomes hot, markedly swollen, and painful with fever.

FNP reasoning: the chronic pattern is concerning for inflammatory polyarthritis and needs prompt rheumatology assessment, but the acutely hot febrile knee is a separate emergency concern for septic arthritis or crystal disease. Do not assume every new joint symptom is an RA flare. Arrange urgent evaluation first, then coordinate definitive inflammatory-arthritis workup and function-centered care.

FNP Inflammatory Arthritis Framework

  1. Classify the pattern: inflammatory versus mechanical, mono- versus polyarticular, acute versus chronic, systemic features, and exposures.
  2. Exclude emergency disease: septic joint, acute crystal disease, fracture, neurovascular compromise, and systemic infection.
  3. Refer early when warranted: persistent synovitis/polyarthritis or functional decline needs rheumatology collaboration.
  4. Protect medication safety: DMARD/biologic indication, screening, labs, infection precautions, reproductive issues, interactions, and access.
  5. Preserve function and health: therapy/devices, cardiovascular prevention, osteoporosis/fall risk, vaccines, mood, work, and shared goals.

High-Yield Summary

Inflammatory pattern: swelling, warmth, prolonged stiffness, rest pain, fatigue, and multi-joint involvement—but differential remains broad.
Hot swollen joint: assess urgently for septic arthritis; absence of fever does not rule it out.
RA: is systemic and early DMARD-directed rheumatology care protects joints and function.
DMARD/biologic safety: requires infection awareness, appropriate screening/monitoring, vaccination planning, access, and team communication.
FNP standard: avoid missed infection, prevent delayed RA treatment, and support safe lifelong function-focused care.

Clinical safety note: This lesson is educational. Arthritis diagnosis, joint aspiration/infection evaluation, DMARD/biologic prescribing and monitoring, vaccination, reproductive counseling, referral, and emergency disposition must follow current guidelines, local policy, collaboration/scope requirements, and the individual patient’s presentation.
